question: Does grouping heterogeneous peers by visit-context similarity and training one model per group beat a single shared model on every peer's held-out data, without leaving low-data peers worse off?
method: Covertype subsample; peers = dominant wilderness area; per-peer stratified 25% test split; k-means on per-peer context summaries; cluster LightGBMs blended per peer with local LightGBMs; baseline shared MLP; seeds 42-44.
baseline: One shared MLPClassifier (64 hidden units) trained on pooled peer training data (FedAvg-style stand-in).
improved: One LightGBM per k-means cluster of peer context summaries (k chosen by silhouette), each peer's prediction = local LightGBM blended with its cluster LightGBM, local weight n_p/(n_p+1000). Fixed hyperparameters (300 trees, lr 0.1, 63 leaves).
notes: Only 4 peers (wilderness areas), so clustering and silhouette selection are very coarse. The improvement comes mainly from the stronger learner (gradient-boosted trees instead of a 30-iteration MLP); the baseline MLP is kept unchanged. The clustering effect alone was not isolated by an ablation. The shrinkage prior (1000) and LightGBM settings were fixed a priori and not tuned on the test set. Small peers lean on the cluster model, large peers on their local model. The improved model fits more models (cluster + local), so it uses more compute. Single data split; results are from one subsample.
